title: The Perils of Rounding Up Students' Answers
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton examines Rounding Up, Doug Lemov's term for a teacher affirming a partly correct answer while quietly supplying the missing critical detail. Using a worked equation exchange with a student called Molly, he argues it is a problem for three reasons: students believe they understand when they do not, standards drop because half-baked answers are accepted, and the teacher ends up doing the hard thinking. His remedy is to push for excellence through a sequence of prompts that lets the student improve her own answer, then checking that other students were listening via Cold Call or Turn and Talk. A second example, sharing money in a ratio, shows a subtler version where a student who says No idea only supplies single numbers while the teacher provides the insight. Suggested responses there include asking what question was set and promising to come back after hearing other students. He concedes the approach takes longer but argues the time creates a classroom where thinking hard is normal.
points: Rounding Up means affirming a nearly right answer and adding the key missing detail yourself, so the teacher rather than the student completes the thinking.
Three costs are named: false confidence in understanding, falling class standards, and the message that the teacher does the hard work.
The fix is to coach the student to improve their own answer step by step, including the correct vocabulary, then have them restate the whole answer.
Listening is checked afterwards with Cold Calling or a Turn and Talk so the improved answer reaches the whole class.
When a student says No idea, supportive but non-rescuing responses keep the student on the hook without the teacher taking over.
quotes: This type of teacher response was a common feature of my teaching for many years, and it prevails in many of the lessons I am lucky enough to see in the schools I now visit.

Rounding Up involves a teacher responding to a partially or nearly correct answer by affirming it, and in so doing, adding critical detail (perhaps the most insightful or challenging detail) to make the answer fully correct.
The standards in the class fall, because students realise they can get away with half-baked answers
Teacher: Let’s improve this answer together. The add 5 does not move, but it does seem to disappear from the left-hand side of the equation. What happens to it?
Sure, this takes longer, but it is more genuine, and addresses each of the three problems outlined above.

The student is clearly contributing to the solution, and what they are saying is correct, but it is the teacher who is once again providing the critical insight. Just like in the solving equation example, there is a real danger that the student (and maybe the teacher) concludes the interaction thinking they understand how to share in a ratio.
Once again, this takes more time. But I think it is time well spent in creating a classroom environment where thinking hard is the norm.
